8. Maghās, the ‘bounties,’ are the Sickle, or α, η, γ, ζ, μ, ε,
Leonis. The variants Anaghā, the ‘sinless one,’ etc., clearly
refer to the auspicious influence of the constellation.
9, 10. Phalgunī, Phalgunyau, Phalgū,^78 Phalgunīs, Phal-
gunyas, is really a-double constellation, divided into Pūrve,
‘former,’ and Uttare, ‘latter.’ The former is δ and θ Leonis,
the latter β and 93 new Leonis. According to Weber, the word
denotes, like Arjunī, the variant of the Rigveda,^79 a ‘bright-
coloured’ constellation.
78) Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, v. 1.
79) x. 85, 13.

Magha in the Rigveda^1 denotes ‘bounty,’ and Maghavan^2 is
the regular Vedic name for the ‘generous giver’ of bounties to
priests. It is doubtful whether the Maghavans were more than
this, or had any special rank as a class in Vedic society. See

) i. 11, 3; 104, 5; iii. 13, 3; 19, 1;
iv. 17, 8; v. 30, 12; 32, 12, etc.;
Nirukta, v. 16. Very rarely later, e.g.,
Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xx. 67.
2) Rv. i. 31, 12; ii. 6, 4; 27, 17;
v. 39, 4; 42, 8; vi. 27, 8, etc. So
Magha-tti, ‘giving of gifts,’ Rv. iv. 37,
8; v. 79, 5; viii. 24, 10, etc.; Magha-
deya, ‘giving of gifts,’ vii. 67, 9;
x. 156, 2; Maghavat-tva, ‘liberality,’
vi. 27, 3. The word Maghavan is the
epithet par excellence of Indra in the
Rv. (iii. 30, 3; iv. 16, 1; 31, 7; 42, 5,
etc.), and survives in post-Vedic litera-
ture as a name of Indra; otherwise,
even in the later Saṃhitās, it is very
rare, occurring practically as a divine
epithet only (of Indra, Taittirīya Saṃ-
hitā, iv. 4, 8, 1; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani-
ṣad, i. 3, 13; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad,
ii. 11).
